x-m-m3-01.title: Testing the claim 'multiplying irrational numbers gives an irrational number'
x-m-m3-01.goal: Test the claim 'multiplying irrational numbers always gives an irrational number' with a counterexample, say how an example that supports it differs in role from a counterexample, and fix the claim.
x-m-m3-01.material: In class, a student claimed, "If you multiply an irrational number by an irrational number, it's always irrational!" For example, √2 is irrational, √3 is also irrational, and their product √6 is also irrational. (√ is read 'root.')
x-m-m3-01.thinking.0: Testing a general claim with a counterexample
x-m-m3-01.thinking.1: Telling 'works in an example' from 'always works'
x-m-m3-01.thinking.2: Rewriting the claim to fit the conditions
x-m-m3-01.prereq.0: That √n (root n) is irrational for a natural number n that is not a perfect square
x-m-m3-01.prereq.1: That an irrational number is a non-repeating infinite decimal and is not a rational number
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.prompt: Make 2 different examples that show this claim is wrong. Choose two irrational numbers √a and √b (a and b are natural numbers from 2 to 200), so that the product √a × √b is a rational number (here, a natural number).
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.hint.0: First decide what kind of numbers a and b must be for √a and √b to both be irrational.
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write what number ends up inside when you combine √a × √b under one root sign, and think about what that number must be for the root sign to disappear.
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.hint.2: Choose one a, then work out which b would make a number when multiplied with a.
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.ok.c1: a and b are natural numbers from 2 to 200.
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.fail.c1: a and b must be natural numbers from 2 to 200.
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.fail.c2: a or b is a perfect square, so its square root is a natural number. Both must be irrational.
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.ok.c3: The product √a × √b is a natural number. You multiplied irrational numbers and got a rational number.
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.fail.c3: The product √a × √b is not a natural number. For what kind of number a×b does the root sign disappear?
x-m-m3-01.s.s1.explain: For example, √2 × √8 = √16 = 4 and √3 × √12 = √36 = 6. Both numbers are irrational but the product is a natural number, so the claim that the product of irrational numbers is always irrational is wrong. (Multiplying the same number, such as √2 × √2 = 2 with a = b = 2, is also a counterexample.)
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.prompt: Another student argued back like this: "√2 × √3 = √6 is irrational, right? With examples like this, even if your counterexample exists, the first claim is still right." How would you evaluate this argument?
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about how many cases you need to check to confirm the words 'always holds.'
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.o.a: Now there is one more example where it holds, so the first claim can be seen as more believable than before
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.r.a: No matter how many examples where it holds you collect, you have not checked 'every case.' Examples cannot 'prove' a claim.
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.o.b: Even a few examples where it holds do not guarantee 'always,' and one example where it fails makes the claim wrong
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.r.b: What decides 'always' is not the number of examples where it holds but whether there is an example that breaks it. An 'always' claim falls with a single counterexample.
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.o.c: It has not been confirmed that √6 is really irrational, so this argument cannot be used as evidence
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.r.c: 6 is not a perfect square, so √6 is indeed irrational. The weakness of the argument is elsewhere.
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.o.d: √2 × √3 can be changed into a fraction before multiplying, so it is rational and this argument is wrong
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.r.d: √2 and √3 are irrational numbers that cannot be written as fractions. The result of multiplying them, √6, is also irrational.
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.explain: A claim that 'it always holds' cannot be confirmed by giving many examples where it holds, but it falls right away with one example where it does not hold. It is true that √2 × √3 = √6 (irrational), but the counterexample √2 × √8 = 4 still stands.
x-m-m3-01.s.s3.prompt: Now rewrite the student's claim in one sentence so that it 'becomes true.' Show with one example why your fixed sentence is correct.
x-m-m3-01.s.s3.hint.0: Think about whether you can keep the word 'always,' and change that word or add a condition.
x-m-m3-01.s.s3.hint.1: To show that your fixed sentence is correct, you can use the example you made earlier together with an example such as √2 × √3.
x-m-m3-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your fixed sentence show both possibilities, that it 'may be rational and may be irrational'?
x-m-m3-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give one example for each of the two possibilities?
x-m-m3-01.s.s3.model.0: Multiplying irrational numbers can give a rational number or an irrational number. For example, √2 × √8 = 4 is rational, and √2 × √3 = √6 is irrational.
x-m-m3-01.s.s3.model.1: We cannot say that the product of irrational numbers is always irrational. √3 × √12 = 6 is rational and √2 × √5 = √10 is irrational, so the result of the product depends on the two numbers.
x-m-m3-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write in sentences, one each, what kind of case must exist for 'it always holds' to be false, and what cases you must check in full for it to be true.
x-m-m3-01.s.s3.model.2: The product of the square roots of two different primes p and q, √p×√q, is an irrational number. For example, √2×√3=√6.

x-m-m3-02.title: Checking a solution that compares 2√3 and 3√2
x-m-m3-02.goal: Find the error made when moving a number outside the root sign inside it, and describe how to check the result yourself.
x-m-m3-02.material: A student solved 'Which is bigger, 2√3 or 3√2?' (2√3 is read '2 root 3,' and 3√2 is read '3 root 2.')
x-m-m3-02.thinking.0: Finding the first wrong line in the solution
x-m-m3-02.thinking.1: Comparing the wrong solution and the correct solution
x-m-m3-02.thinking.2: Checking the result with an estimate or another method
x-m-m3-02.prereq.0: You learned how to move numbers in and out of the root sign to write an expression in the form √(  ) or a√b
x-m-m3-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in this solution.
x-m-m3-02.s.s1.hint.0: Change each line into an approximate value (√2 ≈ 1.41) and check whether the lines before and after have the same value.
x-m-m3-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether line 1 and line 2 look like they were done the same way, and whether they were really done the same way.
x-m-m3-02.s.s1.line.0: Moving 2√3 inside the root sign gives 2√3 = √(2²×3) = √12.
x-m-m3-02.s.s1.line.3: So of the two numbers, 2√3 is bigger.
x-m-m3-02.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. In line 1, 2 was squared (2²) before going in, but in line 2, 3 was multiplied as it is without being squared. 3√2 = √(3²×2) = √18. Lines 3 and 4 are conclusions that inherited this wrong value.
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.prompt: We want to fix line 2 and answer the first question again. Which solution is correct?
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.hint.0: Change both numbers into the form √(  ) and compare the numbers inside the root sign.
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.r.a: You repeated the same mistake of not squaring 3. Check that the approximate value 3√2 ≈ 4.2 differs from √6 ≈ 2.4.
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.r.b: For √12 and √18, the one with the bigger number inside the root sign is the bigger number. Compare again which of 12 and 18 is bigger.
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.r.c: You squared the number outside the root sign when moving it in, and compared the numbers inside the root, 12 and 18, correctly.
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.o.d: We only need to compare the numbers outside the root sign, so 2 < 3. So 3√2 is bigger
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.r.d: The conclusion is the same, but this method ignores the numbers inside the root sign (3 and 2). This method gives a wrong conclusion when the numbers inside the root differ a lot, as with 2√5 and 3√2.
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.explain: 3√2 = √18 and 2√3 = √12, so 3√2 is bigger. A method that compares only the numbers outside the root sign, like choice d, just happens to have the same conclusion and is generally wrong. For example, 2√5 = √20 is bigger than 3√2 = √18, but looking only at the numbers outside the root sign gives 2 < 3.
x-m-m3-02.s.s3.prompt: What check could you do to catch a mistake like this yourself after finishing the solution? Write it concretely for this problem, putting in numbers.
x-m-m3-02.s.s3.hint.0: Before believing that the conclusion of the solution 'seems right,' think about whether you can make the same comparison in another way.
x-m-m3-02.s.s3.hint.1: You can change them into approximate values and compare the two numbers directly, or square both numbers and compare.
x-m-m3-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the check you wrote compare with the result of the first solution (2√3 is bigger) and reveal the error?
x-m-m3-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is it a method you can use for other problems too?
x-m-m3-02.s.s3.model.0: √2 ≈ 1.41 and √3 ≈ 1.73, so 2√3 ≈ 3.46 and 3√2 ≈ 4.23. It is the opposite of the first result, so I can tell something in the solution is wrong.
x-m-m3-02.s.s3.model.1: If I square the two numbers, (2√3)² = 12 and (3√2)² = 18. The one with the bigger squared value is also the bigger original number, so 3√2 is bigger. This way I can tell right away that the first result was wrong.
x-m-m3-02.s.s2.hint.1: Match each choice's conclusion with the sizes of the two numbers that you calculated yourself using approximate values of √2 and √3.

x-m-m3-03.title: When is (a+b)²=a²+b² true?
x-m-m3-03.goal: Find cases where '(a+b)²=a²+b²' holds, guess the condition, and explain the reason by expanding the expression.
x-m-m3-03.material: A friend said, "Isn't (a+b)² just a²+b²?" How to read them: (a+b)² is 'a plus b, squared,' and a²+b² is 'a squared plus b squared.'
x-m-m3-03.thinking.0: Finding examples where it holds and guessing a rule
x-m-m3-03.thinking.2: Expanding the expression to explain the reason for the condition
x-m-m3-03.prereq.0: Multiplying expressions with letters and removing parentheses
x-m-m3-03.prereq.1: Squares and products of negative numbers
x-m-m3-03.s.s1.prompt: Find 3 different integer pairs (a, b) for which (a+b)² = a²+b² really holds, and enter them. (from -20 to 20)
x-m-m3-03.s.s1.hint.0: First, try small numbers such as (a, b) = (2, 3), (1, 1), calculate each side separately, and check whether they are equal.
x-m-m3-03.s.s1.hint.1: If many pairs are not equal, observe for what kind of number the difference between the two values disappears.
x-m-m3-03.s.s1.hint.2: Try changing a or b to 0 or another special number.
x-m-m3-03.s.s1.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from -20 to 20.
x-m-m3-03.s.s1.fail.c2: (a+b)² and a²+b² are different. Calculate the two sides separately and compare.
x-m-m3-03.s.s1.explain: For example, (0, 5), (7, 0), and (0, -3) all work. For (2, 3), the sides are 25 and 13, and for (1, 1), they are 4 and 2, so they differ.
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.prompt: Looking at the pairs you found and the pairs that failed, how would you describe the cases in which this equation holds?
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.hint.0: Find what a and b have in common in the pairs that worked.
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.hint.1: For each choice, put in one pair that can serve as a counterexample and calculate both sides.
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.o.a: When a and b have the same sign
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.r.a: (2, 3) has the same signs, but the two sides are 25 and 13, which differ. Putting in one counterexample rules this out.
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.o.b: When a and b have opposite signs
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.r.b: (3, -3) has opposite signs, but the left side is 0 and the right side is 18. This choice has a counterexample too.
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.o.c: When a and b are the same number
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.r.c: For (1, 1), the sides are 4 and 2, which differ. Being the same number is not the rule.
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.o.d: When at least one of a and b is 0
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.r.d: You caught what the pairs that work have in common. Now it is time to explain 'why it holds only then.'
x-m-m3-03.s.s2.explain: In every pair that worked, a or b was 0. In the pairs where neither was 0, the two sides differed.
x-m-m3-03.s.s3.prompt: Using the method of expanding the expression (a+b)², explain why this equation holds 'only' when a or b is 0.
x-m-m3-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write (a+b)² as (a+b)(a+b) and expand it with the distributive law.
x-m-m3-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the expanded expression with a²+b² and find what part is left over.
x-m-m3-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you go on to write why a or b must be 0 for 2ab to be 0?
x-m-m3-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why they are always different for pairs where neither a nor b is 0?
x-m-m3-03.s.s3.model.0: (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b², so for it to equal a²+b², 2ab must be 0. So they are equal only when one of a or b is 0.
x-m-m3-03.s.s3.model.1: When expanded, 2ab is added to a²+b². This 2ab must be 0 for them to be equal, and for 2ab to be 0, a=0 or b=0.

x-m-m3-04.title: Making b so that x²+bx+12 can be factored
x-m-m3-04.goal: Make values of b yourself for which the quadratic x²+bx+12, whose constant term is 12, can be written as a product of two linear expressions with integer coefficients, and judge why some b are impossible using conditions on the product and sum.
x-m-m3-04.material: In the quadratic x²+bx+12, b is an integer. Find the b for which this expression can be written in the form (x+p)(x+q) using integers p and q. (x² is read 'x squared.')
x-m-m3-04.thinking.0: Making examples that fit the condition yourself
x-m-m3-04.thinking.1: Judging possibility with product and sum conditions
x-m-m3-04.thinking.2: Explaining impossibility by going through all the cases
x-m-m3-04.prereq.1: Divisors of 12 and pairs of integers whose product is 12
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose integers b, p, q so that x²+bx+12 = (x+p)(x+q). Make 3 cases with different b.
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write what x², the coefficient of x, and the constant term become when you expand (x+p)(x+q).
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.hint.1: First choose the product of p and q so that the constant term is 12, then choose b.
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.hint.2: Check whether you can use negative p and q too.
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.ok.c1: b, p, and q are all integers.
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.fail.c1: b, p, and q must be integers.
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.fail.c2: p×q is not 12. Check whether the constant term is 12.
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.fail.c3: The coefficient b of x differs from p+q. Expand (x+p)(x+q) and check the coefficient of x.
x-m-m3-04.s.s1.explain: The integer pairs with product 12 are (1,12), (2,6), (3,4) and their negative pairs (-1,-12), (-2,-6), (-3,-4) (pairs with the order swapped give the same b). The sums are 13, 8, 7, -13, -8, -7, so b can only be these six values.
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.prompt: Now let b = 5. Can x²+5x+12 be written in the form (x+p)(x+q) with integers p and q?
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.hint.0: For x²+5x+12 = (x+p)(x+q), p and q must satisfy both conditions (product and sum) at the same time.
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.hint.1: List every integer pair whose product is 12 without missing any, find each sum, and see whether 5 comes up.
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.o.a: Yes. 2 and 3 add up to 5, so let p=2, q=3 and write (x+2)(x+3)
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.r.a: You matched only the sum. 2×3=6, which is different from the constant term 12. You must check the product condition too.
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.o.b: Yes. b only has to be an integer, so 5 is possible too, and there is no need to examine it
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.r.b: b being an integer is a different matter from satisfying the product and sum conditions of two integers. Work through the conditions.
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.o.c: No. The sums of integer pairs with product 12 are only ±7, ±8, ±13
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.r.c: You listed all the pairs possible under the product condition and then compared the sums. You showed it is impossible by going through all the possible cases.
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.o.d: We cannot tell. To find p and q that give 5, we have to test every integer one by one
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.r.d: There are only finitely many integer pairs with product 12, so you can list them all without missing any. You do not need to test every integer.
x-m-m3-04.s.s2.explain: There are only 6 integer pairs with product 12 (ignoring order), and their sums are 7, 8, 13 and their negatives. 5 is not among them, so if b=5, it cannot be factored with integers p and q.

x-m-m3-05.title: Why can't we set the factors to 2 and 3 when the product is 6?
x-m-m3-05.goal: Check a solution that solved (x-2)(x-3)=6 with the method used when the product is 0, fix your judgment, and explain under what condition each factor can be set to 0 separately.
x-m-m3-05.material: Chulsoo found the solutions of the equation (x-2)(x-3)=6 like this. "6=2×3, so I can set x-2=2 and x-3=3. So x=4 and x=6!" (x-2 is read 'x minus 2.')
x-m-m3-05.thinking.1: Revising a judgment with new evidence
x-m-m3-05.thinking.2: Explaining the condition for applying a method
x-m-m3-05.prereq.0: How to find the solutions of (x-a)(x-b)=0
x-m-m3-05.prereq.1: How to try values in an expression
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.prompt: The materials are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your thought about Chulsoo's solution.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.hint.0: Compare whether the new material from each step supports or opposes your earlier judgment.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.hint.1: When you doubt whether a value is a solution, put it into the original equation and check.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.info: Chulsoo set x-2 to 2 and x-3 to 3 so that the product is 6. But if x-2=2 then x=4, and if x-3=3 then x=6.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think of Chulsoo's solution?
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.after: It is a strange sign when expressions in the same x give different values. In this case, it is good to put them into the original equation and check.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: He set the factors to 2 and 3 so the product is 6, so this solution seems right
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 2 and 3 are not the only two numbers with product 6. There are also 1 and 6, and -2 and -3.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: No x satisfies both x-2=2 and x-3=3 at once, which is strange. I want to put values in and check
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You doubted whether two expressions can give different values for the same x. This is a good judgment, going from doubt to checking.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Two x values came out, which matches the fact that a quadratic equation has two solutions, so it is right
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The fact that two solutions came out is not enough to say it is right. The values must actually satisfy the equation.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is wrong. A quadratic equation cannot be solved when the product is 6
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: A quadratic equation can be solved. First you need to check whether the method Chulsoo used is the problem.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Putting x=4 into the original equation gives (4-2)(4-3)=2×1=2, and putting in x=6 gives (6-2)(6-3)=4×3=12. The right side of the original equation is 6.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now how do you judge Chulsoo's solution and answer?
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.after: x=4 and x=6 are both not solutions. Revise your judgment: Chulsoo's solution is wrong.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The two values do not satisfy the equation, so the solution is wrong
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You revised your judgment using the substitution result as evidence. Values other than 6 (2 and 12) came out, so neither value is a solution.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It might be a calculation mistake, so I think Chulsoo is right
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You ignored the results you calculated yourself (2 and 12). You can check the calculation one more time, but you must not erase the result.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: x=4 is wrong but x=6 might be a solution
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Putting in x=6 gives 12, not 6. It is not an x that makes it 6.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Chulsoo is wrong, but taking the product as 6 might sometimes work
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Whether a method sometimes works and sometimes does not has to be worked out by comparing with the case where the product is 0. With the evidence now, we only know that Chulsoo's answer is wrong.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Minji expanded the expression to get x²-5x+6=6, that is, x²-5x=0, and from x(x-5)=0 got x=0 or x=5. Putting in x=0 gives (-2)(-3)=6, and putting in x=5 gives 3×2=6.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.after: If the product is 0, one factor must be 0, but if the product is 6, the values of the two factors can split in many ways. So we expand, make the right side 0, and then solve.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: x=0 and x=5 are solutions. The method of setting each factor to 0 separately can be used only when the product is 0
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You confirmed by substitution that they are solutions, and also summed up the condition that the method of setting the factors separately can be used only when the product is 0.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: x=0 and x=5 are solutions, and Chulsoo's method can always be used whatever the product is
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Chulsoo's method already gave wrong answers. Think about why it does not work when the product is 6 but works when it is 0.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: x=0 is 0, so it cannot be a solution. The only solution is x=5
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Putting in x=0 gives (-2)(-3)=6, so the equation holds. There is no condition that a solution must be positive.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Minji was just right by chance, and trying values is meaningless
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Trying values lets you check whether something is a solution or not. This method is also what filtered out Chulsoo's answer.
x-m-m3-05.s.s1.reflect: At first it looked like a 'plausible solution,' but how did your judgment change with one substitution? What kind of mistake does the habit of putting in values to check after finding solutions prevent?
x-m-m3-05.s.s2.prompt: To help Chulsoo understand, explain why you may set each factor to 0 separately when the product is 0 but not when the product is 6.
x-m-m3-05.s.s2.hint.0: Find a few possible cases for two numbers whose product is 0 and for two numbers whose product is 6, and compare them.
x-m-m3-05.s.s2.hint.1: In (x-2)(x-3)=6, write at least two pairs of values that x-2 and x-3 could be.
x-m-m3-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write that when the product is 0, 'one factor must be 0'?
x-m-m3-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you give an example showing that pairs with product 6 are not only 2×3?
x-m-m3-05.s.s2.model.0: If the product is 0, one of the two must be 0. But two numbers with product 6 are not only 2 and 3 but several pairs, like 1 and 6, and -2 and -3. So we cannot decide that x-2 is 2.
x-m-m3-05.s.s2.model.1: When the product is 0, there is only one case, that one factor is 0, but when the product is 6, there are many cases like (1,6), (2,3), (6,1), so we cannot know what x-2 and x-3 each are. So we have to expand, make it 0, and then solve.

x-m-m3-06.title: What should we ask to fix a single quadratic function?
x-m-m3-06.goal: Sort out information that is enough to fix a single equation for the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c from information that is not enough, and decide what extra question to ask when it is not enough.
x-m-m3-06.material: We want to find the equation of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c (a is not 0). (y is read 'y equals a x squared plus b x plus c.') A friend will tell you information about the graph one piece at a time.
x-m-m3-06.thinking.1: Showing different equations when information is not enough
x-m-m3-06.thinking.2: Deciding what extra question is needed
x-m-m3-06.prereq.0: That the graph of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c (a≠0) is a parabola
x-m-m3-06.prereq.1: The vertex and axis of a graph, and the coordinates of a point
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information from the following from which the equation of the quadratic function is fixed to a single one using that information alone.
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.hint.0: Work out whether there are two or more different quadratic functions that fit each piece of information.
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.hint.1: When the vertex, the axis, or points it passes through are given, count how many unknowns are left in the equation.
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.r.a: Even with the same vertex, how wide the parabola opens (a) can differ.
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.o.b: The vertex is (2, -1) and it passes through the point (0, 3)
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.r.b: With a vertex and one more point it passes through, a is fixed and the equation is fixed to a single one.
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.o.c: It passes through the two points (0, 3) and (4, 3)
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.r.c: From two points with the same y-coordinate you can find the axis, but you cannot tell how wide it opens.
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.o.d: The axis is x=2 and the y-intercept is 3
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.r.d: Even with the same axis and the same y-intercept, there are many parabolas with different heights of the vertex.
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.o.e: It passes through the three points (0, 3), (1, 0), (3, 0)
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.r.e: With three different points, a, b, and c are all fixed. You can think of it as two x-intercepts and one point.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.hint.0: First check what number c is fixed to when you put the point (0, 3) into the equation.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.hint.1: Put in the point (4, 3) and write what relationship appears between a and b.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.hint.2: Check whether b is fixed once you choose a, and change a to make another equation.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.ok.c1: a is not 0. It is a quadratic function.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.fail.c1: If a is 0, it is not a quadratic function.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.fail.c2: It does not pass through the point (0, 3). Check whether y is 3 when x=0.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.fail.c3: It does not pass through the point (4, 3). Put in x=4 and check whether y is 3.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.explain: If a=1 then b=-4, if a=2 then b=-8, if a=-1 then b=4; whenever b=-4a and c=3, it always passes through both points. The two points alone do not fix a single equation.
x-m-m3-06.s.s3.hint.0: Compare what feature of the graph changed when you changed a in s2.
x-m-m3-06.s.s3.hint.1: Work out whether knowing one such feature fixes the values among a, b, c that are not yet fixed.
x-m-m3-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the information you ask for fix the value (a) that kept changing in s2?
x-m-m3-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say how many equations there would be with that information, so that the equation is fixed?
x-m-m3-06.s.s3.model.0: I would ask whether it passes through one more point, for example (1, 0). If you know three different points, a, b, and c are fixed to a single set.
x-m-m3-06.s.s3.model.1: I would ask for the y-coordinate of the vertex (or the minimum value). The two points already fix the axis as x=2, so if I know the y-coordinate of the vertex, a is fixed and the equation is determined as a single one.
x-m-m3-06.s.s1.explain: 'The vertex and one point' is settled by putting (0, 3) into y=a(x-2)²-1, which gives a=1. 'Three points' is settled by putting (0, 3) into y=a(x-1)(x-3), which gives a=1. For the other three pieces of information, neither the value of a nor the height of the vertex is settled, so there are several equations.
x-m-m3-06.s.s2.prompt: You were only told the information 'it passes through the two points (0, 3) and (4, 3)'. Make and enter 2 different quadratic functions y=ax²+bx+c that satisfy all of this information.
x-m-m3-06.s.s3.prompt: The information 'it passes through two points' alone is not enough. If you could ask your friend exactly one more thing, what would you ask? Also write why getting that information settles the equation to just one.
x-m-m3-06.s.s3.model.2: If I ask 'Does it pass through the point (2, -1)?', then 4a-8a+3=-1 gives a=1, so the equation is settled.

x-m-m3-07.title: Checking a solution for the minimum value of y=2x²-8x+3
x-m-m3-07.goal: Find the wrong line in a solution that rewrites the expression in completed-square form, choose a check that exposes the wrong result, and find the correct minimum value.
x-m-m3-07.material: A student found the minimum value of y=2x²-8x+3 like this. (y is read 'y equals 2 x squared minus 8 x plus 3.')
x-m-m3-07.thinking.0: Finding the first error in the solution
x-m-m3-07.thinking.1: Choosing a check that reveals the error
x-m-m3-07.thinking.2: Stating the minimum value from the corrected result
x-m-m3-07.prereq.0: How to change y=ax²+bx+c into the form y=a(x-p)²+q
x-m-m3-07.prereq.1: The relationship between the vertex of a quadratic function's graph and its minimum value
x-m-m3-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in the student's solution.
x-m-m3-07.s.s1.hint.0: Expand the parentheses and compare line by line whether each line is the same expression as the line right before it.
x-m-m3-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the 2 in front of the parentheses affects the number added inside the parentheses.
x-m-m3-07.s.s1.line.2: The vertex is (2, 3) and the graph opens upward, so the minimum value is 3.
x-m-m3-07.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. A 4 was added inside the parentheses, but since 2 is multiplied in front of the parentheses, 2×4=8 was really added. 8 must be subtracted again. Line 1 is the same as the original expression, and line 3 is a conclusion that inherited the wrong expression of line 2.
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the checks that actually reveal that this solution's conclusion is wrong.
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.hint.0: Actually do the calculation of each check, and compare whether the original expression and the solution's expression give different values.
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.hint.1: A check where the x-coordinate of the vertex is right may not catch an error in the y value.
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.o.a: Put x=2 into the original expression y=2x²-8x+3 to find the y value, then compare it with the solution's minimum value 3
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.r.a: At x=2 the original expression gives 8-16+3=-5, and the solution gives 3. This check reveals the error.
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.o.b: Check only whether the x-coordinate of the vertex, 2, is right
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.r.b: The x-coordinate 2 is right. This check does not reveal the error in the y value (the minimum value).
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.o.c: Put x=0 into the original expression and into the solution's last expression 2(x-2)²+3, and compare whether the two values are equal
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.r.c: The original expression gives 3 and 2(0-2)²+3 gives 11, which differ. This check reveals the error.
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.o.d: Check whether the graph opens upward
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.r.d: It is true that it opens upward. This fact has nothing to do with the minimum value being the wrong size.
x-m-m3-07.s.s2.explain: If the original expression and the solution's expression were the same function, the values would have to be equal at any x. At x=0 they are 3 and 11, and at x=2 they are -5 and 3, which shows the two expressions are different functions. Checks that look only at the x-coordinate or only at the direction it opens miss this error.
x-m-m3-07.s.s3.prompt: Write the vertex and the minimum value found with the correctly fixed solution, and check with one method that it is right.
x-m-m3-07.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate how much the number added inside the parentheses actually adds, and write how to make up for that amount.
x-m-m3-07.s.s3.hint.1: Put x=2 into the original expression to find the y value, and compare it with the corrected result.
x-m-m3-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that the vertex is (2, -5)?
x-m-m3-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In the check, did you compare with the value you get by putting x=2 into the original expression?
x-m-m3-07.s.s3.model.0: It is 2(x-2)²-5, so the vertex is (2, -5) and the minimum value is -5. Putting x=2 into the original expression gives 8-16+3=-5, so it is right.
x-m-m3-07.s.s3.model.1: When I completed the square, I added 4 inside the parentheses, but there is a 2 in front, so actually 8 was added. So I have to subtract 8, which gives 2(x-2)²-5, and the minimum value is -5. I expanded it and checked again.

x-m-m3-08.title: If sin A=3/5, is it the same even when the triangle gets bigger?
x-m-m3-08.goal: Make several right triangles with the same value of sin A, evaluate two students' claims using the results, and explain why a trigonometric ratio is fixed by the size of the angle.
x-m-m3-08.material: In the right triangle ABC, ∠C=90°, side BC is the side opposite ∠A, side AC is the side next to ∠A (not the hypotenuse), and side AB is the hypotenuse. sin A is read 'sine A' and cos A is read 'cosine A.' In these triangles, sin A=3/5 (3 over 5).
x-m-m3-08.thinking.0: Making several examples that fit the condition
x-m-m3-08.thinking.2: Explaining the reason with similarity or proportion
x-m-m3-08.prereq.0: In a right triangle, sin A=(side opposite ∠A)÷(hypotenuse), cos A=(side next to ∠A, not the hypotenuse)÷(hypotenuse)
x-m-m3-08.s.s1.prompt: Make 3 right triangles with sin A=3/5 whose hypotenuse AB has different lengths. Enter the side lengths AB (h), BC (o), and AC (a). (Decimals are fine.)
x-m-m3-08.s.s1.hint.0: As the simplest example, when BC=3 and AB=5, find the length of the remaining side AC with the Pythagorean theorem.
x-m-m3-08.s.s1.hint.1: Keep the ratio 3:5 of BC to AB, increase both to 2 times and 3 times, and check how the remaining side changes.
x-m-m3-08.s.s1.fail.c1: The side lengths must be greater than 0.
x-m-m3-08.s.s1.ok.c2: ∠C is a right angle (the Pythagorean relationship holds).
x-m-m3-08.s.s1.fail.c2: BC²+AC² is not equal to AB². It is not a right triangle.
x-m-m3-08.s.s1.explain: If you enlarge all three sides by the same multiple, as in (AB, BC, AC)=(5, 3, 4), (10, 6, 8), (15, 9, 12), sin A=3/5 stays the same.
x-m-m3-08.s.s2.prompt: There are two students' claims. Minsu: "If the hypotenuse becomes 2 times, sin A also becomes 2 times." Seoyeon: "If sin A is the same 3/5, cos A is always the same too." How do they look when you evaluate them using the triangles you just made?
x-m-m3-08.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate sin A and cos A for (5, 3, 4) and (10, 6, 8) and compare them.
x-m-m3-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check what value AC÷AB comes out as in the three triangles.
x-m-m3-08.s.s2.r.a: In (10, 6, 8), sin A=6/10=3/5 stays the same, so Minsu's claim is not right.
x-m-m3-08.s.s2.r.b: Even if the hypotenuse becomes 2 times, BC also becomes 2 times, so sin A stays the same. Check Seoyeon's claim with the triangles you made too.
x-m-m3-08.s.s2.r.c: Even when the hypotenuse differed, sin A and AC÷AB (cos A) were all the same. You judged each student's claim by weighing it against evidence.
x-m-m3-08.s.s2.r.d: Check Seoyeon's claim with the triangles you made. AC÷AB was 4/5 in all of them.
x-m-m3-08.s.s2.explain: All three sides grow by the same multiple, so sin A does not change (Minsu is wrong). Also AC÷AB was 4/5 in all of them (Seoyeon is right).
x-m-m3-08.s.s3.prompt: Explain why Seoyeon's claim (if sin A is the same, cos A is the same too) holds not only for the triangles you made but for any right triangle.
x-m-m3-08.s.s3.hint.0: If sin A=3/5, you can set BC=3k and AB=5k (k is positive). Find out what AC becomes then.
x-m-m3-08.s.s3.hint.1: From the point of view of similarity, think about how two right triangles are related if ∠A has the same size in both.
x-m-m3-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give the reason that 'the ratio of the three sides is fixed'?
x-m-m3-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use either a way to show triangles of every size at once with k, or similarity?
x-m-m3-08.s.s3.model.0: If sin A=3/5, we can set BC=3k and AB=5k. By the Pythagorean theorem AC=4k, so cos A=4k/5k=4/5, which is always the same.
x-m-m3-08.s.s3.model.1: If ∠A has the same size, the two right triangles are similar. The ratio of similarity is the same, so the ratios of the sides are the same, and so cos A is also the same, 4/5.

x-m-m3-09.title: When the central angle is 100°, is the inscribed angle always 50°?
x-m-m3-09.goal: When using the relationship between an inscribed angle and a central angle for one arc, learn that the inscribed angle can differ depending on which arc of the circle point C is on, and find all the possible values.
x-m-m3-09.material: There are two points A and B on circle O, and the central angle ∠AOB=100° (100° is the central angle for the minor arc AB). Pick another point C on the circle (a point different from A and B) and think about the size of ∠ACB. How to read it: ∠ACB is 'angle A C B.'
x-m-m3-09.thinking.0: Checking a generalization together with its conditions
x-m-m3-09.thinking.1: Splitting into cases and finding all possible values
x-m-m3-09.prereq.0: That the inscribed angle for an arc is half of the central angle for that arc
x-m-m3-09.prereq.1: The central angle of a full turn is 360°
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.prompt: A student said, "The central angle is 100°, so no matter where C is on the circle, ∠ACB is always 50°." How would you evaluate this statement?
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.hint.0: Mark one point C on the major arc and one on the minor arc, and compare which arc ∠ACB faces in each case.
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.hint.1: Check that 'the inscribed angle for an arc' is the angle seen from a point on the opposite side of that arc.
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.o.a: Right. The inscribed angle is half of the central angle, so it is 50° everywhere
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.r.a: For it to be 'half of the central angle,' you must check which arc the inscribed angle faces. See whether the arc it faces changes with the position of point C.
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.o.b: No. As C gets closer to A or B, ∠ACB keeps getting bigger or smaller, so there is no fixed value
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.r.b: While C moves along the same arc, ∠ACB does not change. The value changes when the arc changes.
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.o.c: No. ∠ACB can differ depending on which arc of the circle C is on
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.r.c: You suspected a situation where the arc the inscribed angle faces depends on the position of the point. Now you need to find all the possible values.
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.o.d: Right. ∠AOB and ∠ACB look at the same two points A and B, so they are always the same 100°
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.r.d: An inscribed angle and a central angle have different sizes for the same arc. Looking at the same two points does not make them the same size.
x-m-m3-09.s.s1.explain: The inscribed angle is decided by 'the arc it faces.' If C is on the major arc, it faces the minor arc AB, so it is 50°, half of 100°, but if C is on the minor arc, it faces the major arc AB (260°), so it becomes 130°.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.prompt: Point C can be placed in many places on the circle. Enter 2 different possible values (in degrees) of ∠ACB.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.hint.0: Points A and B divide the circle into two arcs. First find the central angle of each of the two arcs in degrees.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.hint.1: Decide which arc ∠ACB faces when C is on each arc.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.ok.c1: This is the possible range for an angle seen from a point on the circle.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The angle is out of range. It must be greater than 0° and less than 180°.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.ok.c2: This value can actually come up depending on the position of C.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.fail.c2: This value cannot come up. Find the inscribed angle when it faces the minor arc and when it faces the major arc.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.explain: If C is on the major arc, ∠ACB=50°, and if it is on the minor arc, ∠ACB=130°. No values other than these two can come up.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why two values come up.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the central angle of each of the two arcs into which A and B divide the circle, in degrees.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Connect how the arc it faces changes depending on which arc C is on.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the sizes of the two arcs (100°, 260°)?
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: In each case, did you connect that the inscribed angle is half of the arc?
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.because.model.0: If C is on the major arc side, it is the inscribed angle for the minor arc AB (100°), so it is 50°, and if C is on the minor arc side, it is the inscribed angle for the major arc (260°), so it is 130°.
x-m-m3-09.s.s2.because.model.1: The circle can be divided into a 100° arc and a 260° arc. Depending on which arc C is on, the arc it faces is 100° or 260°, so the inscribed angle is half of that, 50° or 130°.

x-m-m3-10.title: Two classes with the same mean: are they really the same?
x-m-m3-10.goal: Compare the distributions of two data sets with the same mean step by step and revise your judgment, and explain that when the spread differs, the conclusion can differ even with the same mean.
x-m-m3-10.material: Class A and Class B each have 6 students. The teacher said, "The mean math score of both classes is 70 points." Starting from this information, you will look at the score data a little more at a time.
x-m-m3-10.thinking.0: Telling what can and cannot be said from the mean alone
x-m-m3-10.thinking.1: Revising a judgment with new data
x-m-m3-10.thinking.2: Correcting and explaining the statement that the means are the same
x-m-m3-10.prereq.0: The meaning of mean, variance, and standard deviation
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed step by step. Each time, choose your thought about the two classes.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new data appears, compare with your earlier judgment and check whether there is a reason to change it.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.hint.1: Besides the mean, compare the maximum, the minimum, and how spread out the scores are.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.info: The mean of both classes is 70 points.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this information alone, what can we say about the distribution of scores in the two classes?
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.after: The mean summarizes the data with one value, so it cannot tell us how spread out the scores are. We need more information.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The means are the same, so the score distributions of the two classes will also be almost the same
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Even with the same mean, whether the scores are bunched together or spread out can differ.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We cannot know the spread, so we cannot say the distributions are the same
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You separated out what the mean cannot tell us. It is the starting point for thinking about what more information is needed.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Even if the mean is 70, there can be students with 50 or 90 points.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.o.d: If the means are the same, the median and the mode must also be the same
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The three representative values can differ from each other. The same mean does not mean the same median.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.info: Here is the score table. Class A: 50, 60, 70, 70, 80, 90 / Class B: 68, 69, 70, 70, 71, 72
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at the table, how would you compare the two classes?
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.after: The means are the same, but Class A is spread out (standard deviation about 12.9 points) and Class B is bunched together (about 1.3). Revise your judgment to 'the distributions are very different.'
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Class A is wide, from 50 to 90 points, and Class B is bunched between 68 and 72 points. The distributions are different
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You revised your judgment by comparing the range and the spread in addition to the mean.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Class A has a 50, so Class A is the weaker class
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You looked only at the low score. Class A has a 90 too. The means are the same.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The means are the same, so as I first thought, the two classes are the same
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Looking at the table, the score distributions of the two classes are noticeably different. Try to reflect the new data in your judgment.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Every student in Class B has a higher score than every student in Class A
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The top score in Class B is 72 points and Class A has 80 and 90. If you compare all the students, that is not so.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.2.info: The teacher said, "I will gather only the students with 80 points or more for an advanced class."
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which class will the students come from? If you had judged only by the mean, what problem would there have been?
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.2.after: Class A has 80 and 90, so 2 students qualify, and Class B has none. When the purpose is 'choosing students with high scores,' you have to look at the distribution even if the means are the same.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 2 students from Class A (80 points and 90 points). Even if the means are the same, you need to look at the distribution to know
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You read the table and counted the actual number of students, and connected the limit of judging by the mean alone to the purpose.
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Class B. The scores are evenly high, so more students qualify
x-m-m3-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Class B scores are 68 to 72 points, so there are no students with 80 points or more. Being evenly bunched does not mean high.
